sections.title: Key topic 1: Queen, government and religion, 1558–69

topics.title: The Situation on Elizabeth's Accession
points: Elizabethan England in 1558: **society and government**.
The Virgin Queen: the problem of her **legitimacy, gender, marriage**. Her character and strengths.
Challenges at home and from abroad: **financial weaknesses, religious divisions, the French threat**.
topics.narrative_blurb: Ascending the throne in 1558, Elizabeth governed a deeply stratified **society and government**. Her rule was shadowed by fierce questions regarding her **legitimacy, gender, marriage**, yet she possessed formidable intelligence. Elizabeth immediately confronted dangerous structural challenges at home and abroad: acute Crown **financial weaknesses, religious divisions**, and the imminent **French threat** from Scotland.

topics.title: The 'Settlement' of Religion
points: Elizabeth's **religious settlement (1559)**: its features and impact.
The **Church of England**: its role in society.
topics.narrative_blurb: To reconcile a fractured nation, Elizabeth enacted the historic **religious settlement (1559)**, establishing the middle way via the Act of Supremacy and Act of Uniformity with its Royal Injunctions. The newly reformed **Church of England** asserted its central role in society, enforcing national conformity, preaching royal obedience, and conducting village parish administration across England.

topics.title: Challenge to the Religious Settlement
points: The nature and extent of the **Puritan challenge**.
The nature and extent of the **Catholic challenge**, including the role of the nobility, Papacy and foreign powers.
topics.narrative_blurb: The middle way faced aggressive opposition from two extremes. The activist **Puritan challenge** demanded the eradication of all popish vestments and crucifixes. Concurrently, a dangerous **Catholic challenge** gathered momentum, sustained by traditional Northern nobility, Jesuit missionary infiltration, and external encouragement from the **Papacy and foreign powers** like Spain and Catholic France.

topics.title: The Problem of Mary, Queen of Scots
points: **Mary, Queen of Scots**: her claim to the English throne.
Relations between **Elizabeth and Mary, 1568–69**.
topics.narrative_blurb: Fleeing Scottish rebellion in 1568, Catholic cousin **Mary, Queen of Scots** arrived in England, possessing a potent dynastic **claim to the English throne** that attracted disaffected nobles. Delicate relations between **Elizabeth and Mary, 1568–69** deteriorated into permanent house arrest, as Elizabeth wrestled with the profound danger of executing an anointed monarch.

sections.title: Key topic 2: Challenges to Elizabeth at home and abroad, 1569–88

topics.title: Plots and Revolts at Home
points: The reasons for, and significance of, the **Revolt of the Northern Earls, 1569–70**.
The features and significance of the **Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots**.
**Walsingham** and the use of spies.
The reasons for, and significance of, **Mary Queen of Scots' execution in 1587**.
topics.narrative_blurb: Northern Catholic grievances erupted in the **Revolt of the Northern Earls, 1569–70**. Subsequent foreign-backed conspiracies—the **Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots**—sought Elizabeth's assassination, but were systematically dismantled by Sir Francis **Walsingham and the use of spies**, directly culminating in the dramatic trial and **Mary Queen of Scots' execution in 1587**.

topics.title: Relations with Spain
points: Political, religious and commercial **rivalry**.
The significance of **privateering** and the activities of **Drake**.
topics.narrative_blurb: Mounting geopolitical friction ignited deep political, religious and commercial **rivalry** between Tudor England and Philip II's global empire. Protestant-Catholic antagonism intersected with illicit English trade in the Caribbean, where licensed state **privateering** and the lucrative plundering **activities of Drake** seizing Spanish silver fleets brought the two powers to the brink of open war.

topics.title: Outbreak of War with Spain, 1585–88
points: Reasons for deteriorating relations with Spain: English direct involvement in the **Netherlands** and the actions of **Robert Dudley**.
**Drake** and the **raid on Cadiz**: 'Singeing the King of Spain's beard'.
topics.narrative_blurb: Relations collapsed following direct military intervention in the Spanish **Netherlands** under the 1585 Treaty of Nonsuch and the controversial actions of **Robert Dudley**, Earl of Leicester. War became overt in 1587 when Sir Francis **Drake** executed the daring naval **raid on Cadiz**, destroying vital supplies in the famous 'Singeing the King of Spain's beard'.

topics.title: The Armada
points: Spanish **invasion plans**. Key events of the **Spanish Armada**.
The reasons for the **English victory**.
topics.narrative_blurb: Philip II launched colossal **invasion plans** in 1588 to transport Parma's veteran army across the Channel. Through tactical blunders and English fire-ships at Gravelines, the key events of the **Spanish Armada** resulted in disaster. Decisive reasons for the **English victory** included superior gunnery, Drake's nimble galleons, defensive communications, and catastrophic North Sea storms.

sections.title: Key topic 3: Elizabethan society in the Age of Exploration, 1558–88

topics.title: Education and Leisure
points: **Education** in the home and schools.
**Sport, pastimes** and the **theatre**.
topics.narrative_blurb: Humanist ideas drove an expansion of grammar school **education** for wealthy boys, literacy, and dame schools, while girls remained confined to domestic tuition. Elizabethan leisure reflected social hierarchy, from violent **sport, pastimes** like bear-baiting and hawking to the wildly popular secular flowering of purpose-built public **theatre** featuring Marlowe and early Shakespeare.

topics.title: The 'Problem' of the Poor
points: The reasons for the increase in **poverty and vagabondage** during these years.
The changing **attitudes and policies** towards the poor.
topics.narrative_blurb: Bad harvests, population growth, rack-renting, and sheep enclosure caused a alarming increase in **poverty and vagabondage**. Fear of rural disorder transformed traditional moral condemnation into changing legislative **attitudes and policies**, distinguishing between the 'deserving' and 'idle' poor, and establishing local poor rates through landmark Elizabethan Poor Laws.

topics.title: Exploration and Voyages of Discovery
points: Factors prompting exploration, including the impact of **new technology on ships and sailing** and the drive to **expand trade**.
The reasons for, and significance of, **Drake's circumnavigation of the globe**.
topics.narrative_blurb: Maritime expansion was propelled by revolutionary **new technology on ships and sailing**, including the astrolabe, triangular lateen sails, and the commercial drive to **expand trade** beyond European cloth markets. National prestige surged with **Drake's circumnavigation of the globe** (1577–80), reaping immense plunder and establishing England as a formidable oceanic maritime power.

topics.title: Attempted Colonisation of Virginia
points: Reasons for the **attempted colonisation of Virginia**, including the significance of **Raleigh**.
Reasons for the **failure of the first settlement** in Virginia.
topics.narrative_blurb: Imperial ambitions motivated the **attempted colonisation of Virginia**, spearheaded by Sir Walter **Raleigh** to challenge Spanish hegemony and establish permanent New World bases. Despite intense royal backing, the **failure of the first settlement** at Roanoke resulted from poor planning, hostile Indigenous relations, severe supply starvation, and the complete disappearance of the 'Lost Colony'.
